analysis.one_liner: Tougher federal safety standards for gas and hazardous liquid pipelines, including corrosion testing.
analysis.headline: The pipeline safety bill never got a committee vote and died at the end of the 104th Congress in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Transportation Department to write tougher rules for the pipes that carry natural gas and hazardous liquids across the country. New pipes would have to meet minimum toughness standards, with extra attention to lines in densely populated neighborhoods. Operators would have to mark buried hazardous-liquid and high-pressure lines so they can be identified, and run periodic tests for corrosion and other slow damage that can lead to ruptures. It also would have required regular reviews of the public education program on leak detection and a faster study of how to reduce risks from where pipelines are built.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, work, or go to school near gas and hazardous liquid pipelines, especially in densely populated areas where a rupture can be deadly. Marking requirements would also help emergency responders and excavators avoid striking buried lines.

how_it_helps.text: Requires minimum toughness standards for new pipes in gas and hazardous liquid pipelines, with particular attention to pipes in high-density population areas.
Requires pipelines in class 3 and class 4 locations to be marked so hazardous liquid facilities and high-pressure gas lines can be identified.
Requires pipeline operators to periodically inspect or test for corrosion and other time-dependent damage that could make a pipeline unsafe at its maximum allowed operating pressure.

Requires the Transportation Secretary to assess the leak-detection public education program every two years and to expedite a study of reducing public safety risks in pipeline siting, including building standards.

analysis.who_pays: Pipeline operators — mostly gas utilities and companies moving oil and hazardous liquids — would bear the cost of tougher pipe, marking, and periodic testing, and those costs would tend to flow to customers in rates.

drawbacks.text: The testing, marking, and tougher-pipe requirements fall on pipeline operators, and compliance costs would tend to be passed on to gas and petroleum customers in prices.

The bill delegates the substance to the Transportation Secretary, who writes the actual standards within 180 days to one year, so the real-world effect depends on rules not written yet; the siting provision is only a study, not a rule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — fewer pipeline ruptures, corrosion failures, and excavation accidents in populated areas — is real but hard to quantify, and the compliance costs are real too. The bill is a modest, rule-writing mandate rather than a dramatic overhaul, so both sides of the ledger are moderate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Bradley introduced the Pipeline Safety Enhancement Act of 1995 on March 23, 1995, joined by Sen. Lautenberg.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
No further action was recorded — no committee markup, no floor vote — and the bill expired when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pipeline operators are better off: they never had to meet the tougher pipe, marking, and periodic corrosion-testing requirements, and avoided the compliance costs those rules would have imposed. People living near pipelines did not get the added protections.

for.name: Sen. Bill Bradley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Pipeline Safety Enhancement Act of 1995.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup or reported the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democratic senators sponsored the bill and no Republican support or opposition was ever recorded; the bill died in committee without a vote, so no partisan split ever showed up on the floor.

industries.industry: Gas and hazardous liquid pipeline operators
industries.note: The bill would have required operators to use tougher new pipe, mark hazardous-liquid and high-pressure lines, and periodically test for corrosion. Their interest in avoiding those compliance costs ran directly against the safety protections people near pipelines would have gained.
